newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico's new peso policy works - official.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico's new peso policy works - official.

text.p: A new method unveiled by Banco de Mexico in mid-February to soften speculative pressure on the peso appears to have worked to the central bank's satisfaction, a senior bank official said in an interview.

Banco de Mexico announced last month that it would sell a fixed amount of dollars -- $200 million -- when the peso lost more than two percent of its value against the U.S. currency in a single day. It would continue the sales while the peso kept sliding two percent per day.
The first test of the method came in late February.
Traders said at the time that once the peso hit the intervention level, fear that the central bank would intervene was enough to stop the weakening -- in effect letting the market self-regulate.

"When the market moved the two percent, market players felt the exchange rate was going to rebound, because they knew that there was a mechanism that would create a potential offer (to buy the pesos)," said the senior official, who declined to be identified.
At the same time as threatening to sell dollars if need be, the central bank is also rebuilding its foreign reserves through a monthly auction of options to sell dollars to the central bank.
"We feel that this symmetrical formula of sale and purchase of currency on the part of the central bank, has very beneficial effects," he said.
Mexico's net international assets have grown sharply since the end of last year, already far outpacing the forecast $2.5 billon increase for the year.
Since the end of 1996, assets -- more or less reserves minus money owing to the International Monetary Fund -- have grown about $4.47 billion.

"For a floating rate currency, we think that the amount of reserves that we have is comparable to other countries with economies that have external trade greater than ours," he said. "We are in a reasonable range."
The February run on the peso was triggered by rising long-term U.S. interest rates and worries the U.S. government might not certify Mexico's war on drugs.

The problem was compounded by low Mexican interest rates and a peso that had gained about 35 percent in real terms over the past 15 months. The peso actually lost 2.1 percent on February 27, but the fall came after the 1215 local time (1815 GMT) time limit for central bank interventions.

Previously, the central bank had moved to leave the money markets slightly short when the peso came under pressure -- a sort of moral suasion, with a small monetary penalty, that showed the central bank was serious about stopping currency pressures.
The small movements in the central bank's liquidity objective were enough of a signal that the markets reacted accordingly.
The central bank left the money markets short on three occasions in 1996 to ease sharp movements in the currency.
